claim: Md. Habib Khan (21) of Nabakalas, Matlab Dakshin, Chandpur, borrowed Tk 5.5 lakh and went to Saudi Arabia in November 2023 on a 'free visa' through a Narayanganj broker named Md. Rashed; after working a while at a residential hotel in Mecca he left, then under a local broker got only occasional small jobs with little pay and spent most of his time idle, according to his family and local sources.
target_section: Avoid a "free visa"
why_new: A dated free-visa case showing the local-broker stage in Saudi Arabia; the guide's free-visa section has no such case.

claim: OKUP's survey of 1,084 households of workers who went to Kuwait, Oman, Qatar, the UAE and Saudi Arabia in 2022 (released 19 October 2025) found that 43% got no work, 57% got a work permit, 21% found no work and paid about Tk 1.5 lakh more for an iqama, 4% paid Tk 44,000 to get work, 4% came home at their own cost, and 14% could not pay for a permit or the trip home and stayed on undocumented.
target_section: Avoid a "free visa"
why_new: Five-country survey, not Saudi-only; guide has OKUP's complaint study (47% no permit) but not these outcome shares.

claim: Expatriates' Welfare Secretary Neyamat Ullah Bhuiyan said in October 2025 that the government is pushing, through bilateral agreements, for workers to be sent at the employer's cost.
target_section: Avoid a "free visa"
why_new: Government stance on employer-pays not in guide.

claim: Prothom Alo reported (November 2024) that on 27 March the bag holding the passport and air ticket of Momin Sheikh (45), a Saudi-based migrant from Sirajganj, fell from the Dhumketu Express bound for Dhaka; a fellow passenger called 999 saying he would miss his 2 pm flight to Saudi Arabia without it, the Tangail railway police outpost found that a woman had picked it up, and the bag was handed back to him.
target_section: Before you fly
why_new: The guide lists 999 for emergencies but has no evidence of what it does for a migrant; this is a case of 999 recovering a lost passport before a flight (year inferred as 2024 from a November 2024 article saying 'last 27 March').

claim: ATAB (the Association of Travel Agents of Bangladesh) said in March 2025 that Dhaka-Saudi fares, which reached up to Tk 1,90,000 in December 2024 and February 2025 because of 'group booking schemes', had fallen to Tk 48,000-50,000, with some airlines selling Dammam and Riyadh tickets for as little as Tk 35,000, after the civil aviation ministry's 11 February 2025 directives made a passenger's name, passport details and passport copy compulsory at booking.
target_section: Before you fly
why_new: The guide already has Tk 48,000-50,000 [G0021] and the name-and-passport booking rule [G0020]; this adds the Tk 1.9 lakh peak from group-booked seats, the Tk 35,000 low and the 11 February 2025 directive date. Guide dates the Tk 48-50k fare May 2025; this source is March 2025.

claim: A Prothom Alo check in April 2025 found a direct Dhaka-Jeddah ticket for 1 May 2025 priced at USD 552 (about Tk 67,000), against USD 307 (about Tk 37,500) from New Delhi to Jeddah the same day.
target_section: Before you fly
why_new: Adds a dated Dhaka-Jeddah market fare; the guide gives Tk 48,000-50,000 [G0021], lower than this fare.

claim: The civil aviation ministry's February 2025 directives require tickets to be sold at the Civil Aviation Authority of Bangladesh's approved fares and discounted tickets to be given to migrant workers, and Biman's managing director, Md Safiqur Rahman, said in April 2025 that discounted tickets were being given to workers going abroad.
target_section: Before you fly
why_new: Partly answers the guide's Need to know 'Does the fare still apply?' under item 6 (as of April 2025, from the directive and Biman); gives no amount.

claim: Ticket agencies told Prothom Alo in April 2025 that under the previous Awami League government a ring formed in which Biman itself held back cheap tickets and released only expensive ones, and that this had not fully stopped; the article said trading in Saudi tickets began in late 2024, and people in the sector said ticket blocking had fallen a lot since the civil aviation ministry's February 2025 directives.
target_section: Before you fly
why_new: Explains the late-2024 Saudi ticket racket behind the fare spike; the guide has only the booking rule [G0020].

claim: The minister also said Biman's discounted 'T-class' fares cut Dhaka-Jeddah from Tk 62,000 to Tk 48,000 and Dhaka-Riyadh or Dammam from Tk 53,000 to Tk 48,000.
target_section: Before you fly
why_new: Guide quotes fares of about Tk 48,000-50,000 in May 2025 (G0021); this names the Biman T-class fare.

claim: Lal Mia (54) of Shalikha, Magura, said he paid a broker Tk 1.3 lakh in 2002 to go to Saudi Arabia but could not go, then paid brokers Tk 2.5 lakh for Malaysia in 2006, Tk 3 lakh for Malaysia in 2010 and Tk 3.6 lakh for Dubai in 2012, about Tk 10.5 lakh over the four attempts, selling four bighas of farmland and 12.5 decimals of homestead, and never went abroad or got the money back.
target_section: Before you pay anyone
why_new: Old case (2002), mainly cross-country (repeat victims). Low priority.

claim: Sakibur Rahman (25) of Mohuripara, Pekua, Cox's Bazar, who went to Saudi Arabia on 6 June 2025, died on the spot in a road accident in Mahil city on 23 July 2025 while learning to drive, and a relative was injured, his elder brother told Prothom Alo.
target_section: Driving
why_new: Driving section has blood-money and insurance rules but no case of a new arrival killed while learning to drive; licence/learning rules are a gap.

claim: Nurul Alam (38) of Akbarpara, Adhunagar, Lohagara, Chattogram, who went to Saudi Arabia 18 years earlier, learned tailoring, worked about 10 years at a firm, then ran his own cloth business in Mahail, Abha (Asir province), delivering cloth to shops in his own microbus; a relative said he was killed on the spot on Thursday night in early December 2025 in a collision with a cargo lorry on his way home after deliveries.
target_section: Driving
why_new: Another road death case; also a long-stayer running his own business (the article doesn't say under what status, relevant to tasattur).

claim: On 15 February 2026 five Bangladeshis from Ramganj, Lakshmipur, died when their private car crashed in Abha on the way home after Umrah: Mizanur Rahman (42), who had long run a hotel business in Abha, his wife, two daughters and their driver Mohammad Jilani alias Babor (30); an 11-year-old daughter was seriously injured.
target_section: Driving
why_new: Road-death case; guide has crash liability (Driving) but no cases. Low priority.

claim: Nure Alam (42) and Yunus Mia (43) of Cumilla, friends who ran a business together in Riyadh, died in a head-on collision at Afif on the Jeddah-Riyadh highway on the night of Friday 15 May 2026 while bringing shop goods from Jeddah, a relative said.
target_section: Driving
why_new: Road-death case. Low priority.

claim: Asif Nazrul said on 20 August 2025 that the interim government had shut the private app 'Ami Probashi' and built an integrated government online platform on which BMET issues emigration clearance 100% online.
target_section: Get BMET clearance
why_new: Conflict: the guide's PDO enrolment step (Step 8) still tells workers to enrol through the Ami Probashi app [B0166]; the minister says the app was shut.

claim: In January 2026 Bangladesh's interim government set a special Biman Bangladesh Airlines fare for migrant workers of at least Tk 20,500 one way on the Madinah-Dhaka and Jeddah-Dhaka routes and Tk 42,000 return on Madinah-Dhaka-Madinah and Jeddah-Dhaka-Jeddah, according to the Chief Adviser's press wing.

why_new: Guide has no cheap-fare scheme for workers going home on leave.

claim: The special fare applied to travel to Bangladesh from 18 April to 25 May 2026 and back to Saudi Arabia from 30 May to 30 June 2026, using flights that the civil aviation adviser said usually return empty during Hajj, with a target of 80,000 tickets sold in Saudi Arabia and Bangladesh combined.
target_section: Going home on leave and coming back
why_new: Dates and size of the scheme; a reviewer may want a Need to know on whether it will run again in the 2027 Hajj season.

claim: Civil aviation minister Afroza Khanam told parliament on 18 June 2026 that Biman had set a Tk 20,000 fare for migrant workers on empty Hajj-season return flights from Jeddah and Madinah, against Tk 50,000-55,000 before on the same routes.
target_section: Going home on leave and coming back
why_new: Confirms the scheme in A0 and gives the usual fare.

claim: One of the two Bangladeshis killed in the 10 October 2026 Riyadh airport attack, Md Shahed Ahmmad of Bogura, a plumber with an iqama on a Saudi contractor's Jeddah project, was returning to work through Riyadh after leave in Bangladesh; the other, Md Nasrullah Badarpuri of Cumilla, was an Umrah pilgrim waiting to fly from Riyadh to Jeddah.
target_section: Going home on leave and coming back
why_new: Shows the risk on the Riyadh transit route that workers and pilgrims use to reach Jeddah.

claim: Abul Hossain of Senbag, Noakhali, a tile mason six years in Saudi Arabia, had booked his return ticket three months ahead but his 12 October 2026 Biman flight to Dammam was cancelled, and he said that if he could not go back he would struggle to keep his job.
target_section: Going home on leave and coming back
why_new: Shows the risk to workers on leave when flights stop; the guide's leave section says nothing about that.

claim: Migration research bodies said in October 2026 that a large share of Bangladeshi workers in the Middle East work in construction in extreme daytime heat, which can damage the kidneys, brain and other organs, worsen breathing, heart, diabetes and kidney disease, and cause premature death.
target_section: Hours, rest and leave
why_new: Health risk behind the guide's summer midday work ban (Hours section); not Saudi-specific.

claim: Asif Nazrul said in August 2025 that he had seen migrant workers at one place in Saudi Arabia living in conditions worse than anyone lives in Bangladesh's worst slum.
target_section: Housing, food and health care
why_new: No first-hand official account of housing conditions in the guide.

claim: According to the uncle of one victim, the workers killed in the 9 August 2026 Riyadh sofa-factory fire were asleep in the factory and its main gate was locked from outside, so they could not get out.
target_section: Housing, food and health care
why_new: The guide has nothing on workers sleeping at the workplace or locked-in housing; a relative's account, not an official finding.

claim: According to Motiur Rahman's family, Motiur, a manpower trader from Raninagar, Naogaon, sent Sajib of Talson village, Adamdighi, Bogura, to Saudi Arabia two years earlier, where Sajib got no iqama because of problems with his papers; Sajib's uncle Jahangir Alam said in May 2025 that the company Sajib was sent to had still not given him an iqama and that Motiur had promised one and kept making excuses.
target_section: If a relative or friend offers you a visa
placement: If it turns out to be a free visa (Cases)
why_new: Another no-iqama case after a broker's visa. CONFLICT within sources: this report says Sajib went two years earlier; the next day's report (f180ac18) quotes his father as saying 40 days earlier.

claim: In both October 2024 Barishal cases the victims' fathers filed at the Human Trafficking Offence Suppression Tribunal and the judge ordered the local police station's officer in charge to record the complaint as an FIR; in the first case he also ordered an investigation report.
target_section: If an agency, broker or relative takes your money
why_new: The guide mentions a police case under the trafficking law and a CR case at the magistrate's court [RC0045, RC0021], but not filing directly at the trafficking tribunal, which then orders the police to register it.

claim: The family of cousins Sohel Molla and Iqbal Molla of Jaldia village, Sultanpur union, Rajbari Sadar paid neighbour Moniruddin Molla and his brother-in-law Mamun Molla Tk 6 lakh in cash on 5 March 2024 and Tk 4 lakh through a bank on 26 May 2024 for good jobs in Saudi Arabia, where, the family says, the two got no work and were abused by the broker ring.
target_section: If an agency, broker or relative takes your money
why_new: New case of neighbours acting as brokers (Tk 5 lakh a head, paid partly by bank), adding to the guide's relative/neighbour fraud cases.

claim: Sohel's father Kamal Molla said the brokers took a further Tk 2 lakh from the family on 7 February 2025 on a promise of work for the two men, after which the men lost contact with their families, and Sohel's wife Rina Akter said in May 2025 that the brokers were now demanding Tk 10 lakh more to bring them back.
target_section: If an agency, broker or relative takes your money
why_new: Shows the follow-on demands (money for work after arrival, then money to bring the men home); the guide's free-visa section has post-arrival payments but not ransom-style demands to return a worker.

claim: On 27 April 2025 Rina Akter filed a case under the human trafficking prevention and suppression law against Moniruddin and Mamun at Rajbari's human trafficking offences tribunal, which ordered PBI (the Police Bureau of Investigation) Faridpur to investigate; Mamun said the men had refused to work at the company they were given and their passports were returned from the company through the agency.
target_section: If an agency, broker or relative takes your money
why_new: Example of a family going straight to the trafficking tribunal (complaint case) and the court sending it to PBI; the guide mentions the trafficking law route [RC0045] without a Saudi example of a tribunal filing.

claim: According to the CID, a ring took Tk 6 lakh from a man for a fast-food shop job in Saudi Arabia, sent him there on 7 June 2025 with no job, held him in a house, beat him and demanded more money from his family for an iqama; he escaped, was detained by Saudi police and sent back on 22 July 2026, and his wife filed a human trafficking case at Savar police station.
target_section: If an agency, broker or relative takes your money
why_new: A case of the 'pay more for the iqama' extortion with confinement in Saudi Arabia and a trafficking case filed from home; the guide's section lacks this pattern.

claim: The CID's human trafficking unit arrested ring member Md Salman Hossain (33) at Dhaka's Shahjalal airport on 31 August 2026; the CID said the victim had been held in Salman's own house in Saudi Arabia.
target_section: If an agency, broker or relative takes your money
why_new: Shows a trafficking case leading to an arrest when the accused flew home.

claim: Under Saudi labour law the employer or the Saudi government must bear a worker's cost of going home, and the Saudi human resources ministry's spokesperson Mike Goldstein told the New York Times (abridged in Prothom Alo, March 2025) that under no circumstances will a worker bear the cost of repatriation, but returned workers and labour-rights groups said workers are in practice forced to pay and those who cannot are sometimes held.
target_section: If something goes wrong
placement: under Work visa: domestic worker; other: who pays the ticket home in practice
why_new: The guide says a domestic worker leaving without a valid reason pays her own ticket [D0019]; this adds the ministry's stated rule and the reported practice. The workers in the article are Kenyan and Ugandan, not Bangladeshi.

claim: The Saudi government had tasked an organisation called Sakan with housing and legal help for foreign workers in difficulty; the ministry spokesperson told the New York Times that the government stopped Sakan's funding in 2023 and that another organisation, Samasco, now does this work; three Kenyan women in a Samasco shelter said they would not be allowed home unless each paid USD 400, and Samasco did not respond.
target_section: If something goes wrong
placement: under Work visa: domestic worker; Complain in this order, item 2 (shelters)
why_new: New: names Samasco as the Saudi-funded shelter operator for foreign workers (Sakan before 2023), with an allegation of a USD 400 exit charge; the guide lists only the Bangladesh embassy's safe homes.

claim: Ugandan domestic worker Mary Nisimenta told the New York Times that after she jumped from a three-storey roof in Najran to escape her employer and was treated for a spinal injury, she reported the abuse to the police and the doctor, who told her to go back to work; when she refused, the Saudi placement agency sent her home.
target_section: If something goes wrong
placement: under Work visa: domestic worker; other: reporting abuse to police or a doctor
why_new: Shows what reporting abuse to Saudi police or hospital staff can lead to; the guide does not cover this. Not a Bangladeshi case.

claim: BRAC associate director Shariful Hasan said in December 2025 that brokers and even relatives often effectively sell women domestic workers under the name of sending them free, and that when they are abused abroad, intervention by the embassy or authorities is limited, with no trial and no accountability.
target_section: If something goes wrong
placement: other: domestic workers, what help reaches them
why_new: Evidence on what help actually reaches abused domestic workers (Work visa: domestic worker, If something goes wrong).

claim: Sanjida Akhter of Narsingdi, back from Saudi Arabia in 2025 after 2 months 25 days, said her employer made her work in his own house, his mother's and his in-laws', fed her only bread, and returned her to the Saudi recruiting agency's office when she fell ill, where the abuse began; she paid for her own ticket home and came back empty-handed.
target_section: If something goes wrong
why_new: Case of work in several houses (barred by Saudi rules the guide cites, D0012) and abuse at the recruitment office; target is the If something goes wrong section under Work visa: domestic worker.

claim: An OKUP study in 2025 found that 94% of women workers forced to return had suffered regular physical and mental abuse abroad, 47% sexual harassment, and 82% had worked from dawn to midnight.
target_section: If something goes wrong
why_new: Not Saudi-only (all destinations); target is Work visa: domestic worker, If something goes wrong, or CROSS-COUNTRY: What are a domestic worker's rights?

claim: State Minister for Expatriates' Welfare Md Nurul Haque said in September 2026 that legal aid had been started in 13 countries and a safe home runs in Saudi Arabia, and that abuse had fallen as a result.
target_section: If something goes wrong
why_new: Confirms safe homes still run (guide: Riyadh, Jeddah, Madinah [E0038]); the 13-country legal aid is new but the article gives no how-to.

claim: According to her family as reported by The Daily Star and cited in a Prothom Alo column (17 October 2026), Rizia Begum went to Saudi Arabia in 2019 as a domestic worker, was abused by her employer, lost contact with her family after 2021, and returned to Bangladesh in February 2026 unable to state her own identity at the airport; she was identified and reunited with her family with help from BRAC and the authorities.
target_section: If something goes wrong
why_new: A concrete case of a domestic worker out of contact for years; guide has no such case, and it shows BRAC's airport help in practice.

claim: In September 2026 parliament was told there are two safe homes in Saudi Arabia, according to a Prothom Alo opinion column (17 October 2026).
target_section: If something goes wrong
placement: Complain in this order, item 2 (Work visa: domestic worker)
why_new: CONFLICT: guide says the labour wings run safe homes in Riyadh, Jeddah and Madinah (three) [E0038, E0019].

claim: The Expatriates' Welfare Ministry said in August 2025 that legal consultancy firms had been appointed in Qatar, Oman, Saudi Arabia, the UAE and Kuwait.
target_section: If you aren't paid
why_new: The guide has no mention of a ministry-appointed law firm in Saudi Arabia; name and access route are a gap.

claim: Moyna Begum of Gondogoali, Atrai, Naogaon, said her elder son Mohon went to Saudi Arabia seven years before August 2026 by mortgaging land and borrowing Tk 4 lakh from a samity (savings association), a debt that had grown with interest to Tk 8 lakh, still unpaid when he and his brother died in the Riyadh factory fire.
target_section: If you need to borrow
why_new: Shows a samity loan doubling over seven years; the guide's borrowing section has no such case. The article gives Mohon's age as 22 while 684eb2b4 gives 42.

claim: Shahinur Rahman of Par-Naogaon, Naogaon, borrowed Tk 5.7 lakh from a samity against his homestead land at Par-Boalia to go to Saudi Arabia about five months before he died in the August 2026 Riyadh fire, and his widow said the samity could take the land if the loan is not repaid.
target_section: If you need to borrow
why_new: A 2026 migration cost (Tk 5.7 lakh) and the risk to mortgaged homestead land when a worker dies; not in the guide.

claim: Foreign Minister Hasan Mahmud told parliament on 19 February 2024 that 9,370 Bangladeshis were held in prisons in 26 countries, the most, 5,746, in Saudi Arabia.
target_section: If you or a relative is arrested
why_new: The guide gives no number of Bangladeshis jailed in Saudi Arabia.

claim: Foreign Minister Hasan Mahmud told parliament on 1 July 2024 that 11,450 Bangladeshis were held in prisons in 31 countries, the most, 5,746, in Saudi Arabia.
target_section: If you or a relative is arrested
why_new: Same Saudi figure as the minister gave in February 2024 (article a5eb1d4c); a later date for the same number.

claim: On 30 January 2025 Bangladesh asked Saudi Interior Vice Minister Nasser bin Abdulaziz Al Dawood for help with quick repatriation of irregular migrants and for a royal pardon for Bangladeshi prisoners convicted of minor offences; he said he would review and consider these.
target_section: If you or a relative is arrested
why_new: Royal pardons for minor offences are not in the guide; outcome unknown.

claim: Shakil Mia (28) of Kishoreganj went to Saudi Arabia in 2019 on borrowed money through Altab Recruiting Agency of Banani, Dhaka, left his workplace because of complications with his employer over his iqama (work permit), and was arrested by Saudi police while working illegally and jailed, his uncle said.
target_section: If you or a relative is arrested
why_new: Case of the iqama-to-jail path.

claim: From jail Shakil told his family he needed about Tk 2 lakh for bail to come home, and his father said they borrowed and sent about Tk 1.8 lakh to a lawyer in Saudi Arabia; Shakil died in custody on 15 May 2026 after, his family said, an air conditioner exploded and the smoke left him unable to breathe.
target_section: If you or a relative is arrested
why_new: What families actually pay for bail and a lawyer; guide has a Need to know on legal help.

claim: Prothom Alo (16 October 2026) reported that Bangladesh and Saudi Arabia are both parties to the Vienna Convention on Consular Relations, under whose Article 36 the detaining country must, at the prisoner's request, inform the prisoner's consulate without delay and allow consular assistance; it was not clear whether the two executed Bangladeshis had made that request.
target_section: If you or a relative is arrested
why_new: Guide says Saudi authorities may not tell the embassy, but not that notification is triggered by the prisoner's own request; this changes what an arrested worker should do (ask for the consulate to be told).

claim: According to unofficial sources in Saudi Arabia cited by Prothom Alo (16 October 2026), the trial of the two executed Bangladeshis ran for several months in a Jeddah court, with two Bangladeshi citizens helping as interpreters.
target_section: If you or a relative is arrested
why_new: Guide (G0004) says the court provides an interpreter; this adds that a trial ran for months and that Bangladeshis interpreted, yet the mission did not know.

claim: On 17 October 2026 State Minister for Foreign Affairs Shama Obaid Islam said the labour wing of the Bangladesh mission in Saudi Arabia had reported the two executed Bangladeshis were engaged in 'adultery' inside a Makkah mosque, that the government had received nothing formally, and that how the bodies could be brought back would be known only after Saudi Arabia answered Bangladesh's letter.
target_section: If you or a relative is arrested
placement: Need to know (bodies of executed workers)
why_new: Guide says nothing on what happens to the body of an executed worker.

claim: According to a Prothom Alo column (19 October 2026), a Sri Lankan national sentenced to death in Saudi Arabia in a blasphemy case had the sentence overturned by the Saudi Supreme Court after the Sri Lankan government took diplomatic and legal action, with a special legal team working alongside Saudi lawyers.
target_section: If you or a relative is arrested
why_new: Evidence that legal help with Saudi lawyers can reverse a death sentence; guide has none.

claim: State Minister for Foreign Affairs Shama Obaid Islam was quoted by Bangla Tribune (17 October 2026), as cited in Prothom Alo, saying that when something happens under Saudi law 'there is not much for us to do'.
target_section: If you or a relative is arrested
why_new: Shows the government's stated limits on helping arrested workers; guide's Need to know asks what legal help the embassy gives in practice.

claim: On 19 October 2026 Expatriates' Welfare Minister Ariful Haque Chowdhury said one of the two Bangladeshis executed in Makkah was a migrant worker and the other an Umrah pilgrim, and that their bodies would be brought home once air links and the overall situation normalised.
target_section: If you or a relative is arrested
why_new: CONFLICT: guide (G0001) and the Jeddah consulate's memo say both were cleaners (Al Majal company); the minister says one was an Umrah pilgrim. Also adds the government's stated intent to repatriate the bodies.

claim: According to Bangladesh foreign ministry officials, at a 19 October 2026 meeting in Jeddah the Saudi side said that after the August 2023 arrests a lower court sentenced the two Bangladeshis, an appeal-court panel of 13 judges upheld the death sentences, and they were executed in separate cells for men and women.
target_section: If you or a relative is arrested
why_new: Adds the Saudi court path (lower court, 13-judge appeal panel) not in guide.

claim: According to foreign ministry sources (19 October 2026), the Saudi foreign ministry's list of sentenced prisoners sent to the Bangladesh consulate in Jeddah on 30 September 2026 named Nazrul Islam and Sweety Akter and their offences but not their sentences; the consul general said that had the list shown the death sentences, the mission could have acted to protect them.
target_section: If you or a relative is arrested
placement: If a relative or friend is arrested
why_new: SG0035 says Saudi Arabia sends lists; this adds that the lists can omit the sentence, so a mission may not know a death sentence even when it knows of the detention.

claim: According to government documents and Bangladeshi diplomats (19 October 2026), Nazrul Islam (from Brahmanbaria) and Sweety Akter (from Tangail) went to Saudi Arabia in late 2022 and joined the Al Majal company as cleaners; Nazrul was detained on 1 August 2023 for a cybercrime or IT offence and held in the Jeddah correctional facility, and Sweety on 2 August 2023 for adultery and held in the Jeddah women's prison.
target_section: If you or a relative is arrested
why_new: Adds employer (Al Majal), home districts and prisons; guide (G0001) has the arrest dates and charges.

claim: According to a Prothom Alo column (20 October 2026), in a qisas (retaliation) case only the victim's family can pardon: if it demands compensation, is paid blood money and agrees to forgive, even a person sentenced to death is freed; in 2011 eight Bangladeshi workers were beheaded for killing an Egyptian guard after his family refused Bangladesh's offer of blood money.
target_section: If you or a relative is arrested
placement: other: murder cases and blood money
why_new: Guide mentions the 2011 executions (G0008) and blood money for crashes, but not that in murder cases only the victim's family can pardon in exchange for blood money.

claim: According to a Prothom Alo column (20 October 2026), every year at Ramadan, both Eids and the Prophet's death anniversary Middle Eastern countries let prisoners and minor offenders go home under general pardons, and the Bangladesh consulate in Saudi Arabia regularly applies for royal pardons for Bangladeshis not held for serious crimes.
target_section: If you or a relative is arrested
why_new: Guide doesn't mention royal pardons as a route out of prison.

claim: According to a Prothom Alo column (20 October 2026), in 2021 the governor of Saudi Arabia's Eastern Province spared a Bangladeshi from the death penalty and arranged for him to be sent home.
target_section: If you or a relative is arrested
why_new: A case where a death sentence on a Bangladeshi was lifted; not in guide.

claim: According to a Prothom Alo column (20 October 2026), Bangladesh has sentenced-prisoner transfer agreements only with India (2010) and the UAE (2014), none with Saudi Arabia, although in February 2024 the then home minister said Saudi Arabia was interested in a prisoner repatriation agreement.
target_section: If you or a relative is arrested
why_new: Tells families a Bangladeshi convicted in Saudi Arabia cannot be transferred to serve the sentence at home; not in guide.

claim: According to Nazrul Islam's family (20 October 2026), he went to Saudi Arabia on 10 November 2022 to work as a cleaner at the Haram in Makkah, was arrested about eight months later, the family learned of the arrest a month afterwards, he was able to phone his parents for one to two minutes about once a month from prison, and on the day of execution someone from Saudi Arabia phoned the family to tell them.

placement: If a relative or friend is arrested
why_new: Partly answers the guide's Need to know 'Can an arrested worker call family from custody?': in this case, short monthly calls.

claim: According to a confidential 18 October 2026 letter from the Jeddah consulate's labour welfare wing to the Expatriates' Welfare Ministry, the consulate had asked the Saudi foreign ministry for information on Bangladeshis held in prisons in western Saudi Arabia, and the list it received on 30 September contained no information on the two executed workers' sentences.
target_section: If you or a relative is arrested
placement: If a relative or friend is arrested
why_new: Adds that the consulate obtains prisoner lists on request and they can lack sentences (G0001-G0006 cover the rest of this memo).

claim: ESOHR documented, in cases of foreigners facing death sentences in Saudi Arabia, the absence of professional interpreters, no legal aid, defendants not understanding the proceedings and no effective chance to defend themselves; prisoners said death-row inmates were briefly isolated and cut off before being taken suddenly for execution (Prothom Alo, 22 October 2026).
target_section: If you or a relative is arrested
why_new: Guide (G0004) says interpreters are provided; this documents interpreter and legal-aid gaps in capital cases.

claim: The Saudi foreign ministry's list of 30 September 2026 named 2,461 Bangladeshi prisoners in the Jeddah consulate's area; for 22 of them, including the two executed, the status column said 'sentenced' but the judgment-summary column was blank, and the 22 cases comprised 8 murder, 5 drug trafficking, 5 'private right', 2 state-law violations, 1 cybercrime and 1 adultery case (Prothom Alo, 22 October 2026).
target_section: If you or a relative is arrested
